newsitem.title: UK: Albania gets its looted Nazi gold back, at last.
newsitem.headline: Albania gets its looted Nazi gold back, at last.

text.p: The fate of one and a half tonnes of Albanian gold looted by the Nazis during World War Two was finally settled on Tuesday after nearly 50 years of diplomatic wrangling.

The gold, worth $19 million, has languished in the vaults of the Bank of England since 1947 mainly because of a dispute over compensation for an incident a year earlier when two British warships hit mines off the Albanian coast, killing 44 sailors.

The British government said it transferred ownership of the gold to Albania following a meeting between the governor of the country's central bank, Kristaq Luniku, and officials of the Tripartite Gold Commission -- made up of wartime allies Britain, France and the United States.
"The matters remaining in dispute between the UK and Albania have now been settled," a spokesman for the Foreign Office said.
"This is a historic day for Albania and for our bilateral relationship. It marks the end of our dispute on this issue with the previous regime," he added.

Britain demanded compensation for the sinking of the warships but Albania's hardline Communist leaders denied responsibility and negotiations did not begin in earnest until democracy was restored in 1991.
Tirana agreed in May 1992 to pay some $2 million, prompting Britain to lift its block on the return of the gold, which the Nazis looted from Albania's central bank in 1945.

The United States followed Britain's lead in 1995 after it settled outstanding claims against Albania, and France gave its approval for the restitution of the gold last February -- paving the way for the start of legal procedures that were completed at Tuesday's talks in London.

At the same time as Albania made an electronic payment of the agreed compensation of $2 million, Britain transferred formal ownership of the looted gold, which officials said was likely to stay for now on deposit at the Bank of England.

"This is the last major single share of the Commission's gold pool to be settled," Emrys Davies, the secretary-general of the panel, said in a statement. "The Commission will now proceed with preparations for the final distribution of the remaining gold in the pool to the claimant governments."

The Commission, formed in 1946 to distribute Nazi gold recovered by the Allied forces, has some 5-1/2 tonnes of gold worth about $70 million on deposit at the Bank of England and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

The gold will be shared out among the governments of Belgium, Italy, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Poland, Austria, Yugoslavia and Greece as well as Albania -- plus the successor states of Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia.

Once the final distribution is complete, the Commission's work will be done and it will be wound up -- ironically, just as efforts are being stepped up to trace any Nazi gold still held in Swiss bank vaults.
